items.title: 8.3 Relation between macroscopic and microscopic events

source_refs.note: Topic 8.3, printed page 170, with Quick Check 8.1.

blocks.text: Macroscopic events are the result of multiple simultaneous microscopic events. Understanding the microscopic events helps us to explain and predict the observed macroscopic changes in the equilibrium system.

When a change in equilibrium occurs in a chemical reaction, the microscopic events that explain the observed changes in equilibrium are the collisions and formation of new bonds between particles or molecules. These collisions change the rates of forward and reverse reactions, which are affected by activation energy and external factors. These microscopic events collectively appear as macroscopic changes which are observable by naked eye.

blocks.prompt: a) Differentiate between macroscopic and microscopic events
blocks.explanation: The differences are given in the table. A macroscopic change is the sum of very many microscopic events.

rows: Not visible to the naked eye
The combined effect of very many particles
Take place at the level of individual particles (atoms, molecules, ions)
Examples: a change of colour, release of heat, formation of a precipitate, evolution of a gas, a change of pressure
Examples: collisions of molecules, breaking and forming of bonds, transfer of electrons

blocks.prompt: b) The equilibrium is dynamic in nature, explain in terms of microscopic events.
blocks.explanation: At equilibrium no change is seen, yet reactant molecules are still colliding, breaking bonds and forming products, and product molecules are also colliding and re-forming reactants. Both processes go on at exactly the same rate, so the composition of the mixture stays constant while the molecules never stop moving.

blocks.prompt:
c) In the reaction H₂O(g) + CO(g) ⇌ H₂(g) + CO₂(g), the concentration of the products is higher at the equilibrium stage.
i. Plot a graph between concentrations of reactants and products and time.
ii. Plot a graph between rate of the reaction with respect to time.
blocks.explanation: (i) The H₂O and CO curves start high and fall; the H₂ and CO₂ curves rise from zero. After equilibrium all the curves become flat, with the product curves above the reactant curves. (ii) The forward rate starts at its highest and falls; the reverse rate rises from zero; the two meet and continue as one flat line (see the rate graph of topic 8.2).

answer_figure.alt: Two graphs. (i) Concentration against time: blue curves [H₂O] or [CO] fall from high values, red curves [H₂] or [CO₂] rise from zero; after the dashed 'equilibrium' line both become flat, with red (products) above blue (reactants). (ii) Rate against time: the red forward rate falls from high, the blue reverse rate rises from zero; at equilibrium they meet in one flat line (forward = reverse).
answer_figure.caption: Answer diagram: (i) concentration–time and (ii) rate–time graphs for H₂O + CO ⇌ H₂ + CO₂ when products are favoured at equilibrium
answer_figure.long_description: Upper graph (i): at the start only H₂O and CO are present, so their concentration is high and that of the products is zero. As the reaction proceeds, the reactants decrease and the products increase; after equilibrium the concentrations stop changing and the products line stays above the reactants line, because the products are favoured. Lower graph (ii): the forward rate falls as the reactants are used up and the reverse rate rises as the products build up; at equilibrium the two are equal and form one flat line (dynamic equilibrium).
